summary: Pathfinders42 is a web application that, for every place where we want to land or build a base on the Moon or Mars, finds its best analogs on Earth and explains how they are similar, how closely, and where the analogy breaks down. We compare 160 sites (the 9 Artemis candidate regions, 29 lunar landing sites, 59 Mars sites and 63 caves and pits) with 117 places on Earth. The comparison uses physical measurements from open data by NASA and other agencies: topography, surface temperature, geology, ice and permafrost, and cave shape. Results can be ranked by mission use: landing, mobility, regolith construction, thermal testing, water and ice, and caves. A machine learning model (LightGBM with positive-unlabeled learning, explained with SHAP) also scans the whole planet and proposes 27 regions that nobody had suggested as analogs before. Known analogs (Atacama, Haughton, Death Valley) are few and not fully characterized. We offer a reproducible and explainable way to decide where to test equipment and train crews before flight.
details:
What it does and how it works

  1. Data: in Google Colab we download and process satellite data of the Earth, the Moon and Mars (NASA Earthdata, PDS, USGS, ESA) and reduce it to small, precomputed files.
    • slope and relief (Kolmogorov-Smirnov test on their distributions),
    • surface temperature (percentiles),
    • rock type (fraction of shared rock),
    • subsurface ice,
    • cave shape (depth/diameter ratio).
    • When we hide a known analog from the model, it puts it back, on median, in the top 4% of the planet.
    • Six volcanic fields it never saw all land in the top 5%.
    • It proposes 27 new regions (Afar, Turkana, the Pamirs, Changtang, Payenia…), each with a SHAP explanation of why it was selected.
  2. Web app: a FastAPI backend deployed on Render and a React + TypeScript frontend deployed on Vercel. It includes a map, a detail card for each site, a mission-use selector and an assistant that answers questions using the project’s data.

Benefits and impact
Mission teams can choose an analog for each mission and use, and know in advance what cannot be tested there. They can also discover alternatives to the usual sites that are closer or cheaper. The method is reproducible: every number comes from public data, and every “verified” analog has a source that presents it as such. It is also useful for teaching and outreach.

Key results

  • Artemis: all 9 Artemis candidate regions have an analog. Massifs resemble Lofoten (Norway) and plateaus resemble White Mountain (Greenland), two anorthosite outcrops like the lunar highlands. Before we added the anorthosite layer, none of them had a match.
    • Mons Mouton is the only site with a robust hydrogen signal.
    • Haworth combines cold temperatures, hydrogen and low roughness.
    • The Pamirs emerge as an ice-and-terrain analog for Nobile Rim 1, although they were not among the known analogs.
  • Mars: all 59 sites have a terrain match. Atacama ↔ Jezero is one of the strongest (0.060).
  • Caves: under the overhangs of lunar pits the temperature is about 17 °C, very close to what is measured next to the Mauna Loa lava tubes (HI-SEAS).

Tools

  • Data and model: Python (pandas, numpy, xarray, scipy, rasterio, shapely, earthaccess), Google Colab and Google Drive, LightGBM and SHAP.
  • Web: FastAPI and Pydantic (backend on Render), React and TypeScript (frontend on Vercel).
  • Assistant: Groq with the open model gpt-oss-120b.
  • Team: GitHub for code and task management.

Creativity

  • We do not compare images. We compare equivalent physical measurements on the three bodies, so every comparison can be explained.
  • Every analogy states where it works, how well and where it fails, layer by layer and in °C.
  • We use positive-unlabeled learning because there are no confirmed “non-analogs”: a place nobody has studied may still be a good analog.
  • We include the subsurface (caves by type, and ice) and the anorthosite of the lunar south pole, which global geologic maps of the Earth do not distinguish.

Factors we considered

  • Scale: from about 240 m to about 50 km depending on the layer.
  • Source reliability: an analog counts as “verified” only if a source backs it.
  • Model bias with few examples: monotonic constraints, minimum spacing between candidates and spatial validation.
  • The limits of the Earth as an analog.
  • Data licenses.
  • Cost: the web app only serves precomputed results.
  • Reproducibility: every version logs its data, thresholds and metrics.
